items.author: Aaron Levie
items.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
items.summary_en:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

items.summary_en:
big boy

warm tension, cold chills
heart hanging off a cliff, ready to free fall
floating in space with no love, just me and some stranger souls
wearing smiles and greet “How are you?”
“I’m good, you?”

life carries on, unhinged
a tear slips, no one noticed
vision blurs, drowned in thoughts
what a strange grown-up world

i asked my inner child, why do you live?
he has never thought about it
he slid on the cold iced river, amused
he sang, he played, he drew
he flew into the unknown, fearless, curious
he closed his eyes and saw wonders

like water, with no shape
like paper, clear of rules

“Why cry, big boy?”
“You are still me, and I’m still you.”

items.author: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
items.title: State of AI 2026: The Biggest Stories of the Year (and AGI in 2027?) | Nathan Benaich
items.summary_en:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:18
The cyber risk is, like, much more real than, like, AI exterminating humanity. You either, like, die trying to get to the frontier or you just live long enough to eventually serve inference. Individuals would prefer to live next to a nuclear power plant than live next to a data center. It's bananas what's happened in the last year alone, so let's see AGI next year.

Speaker 2 | 00:18 - 00:54
That is Nathan Beneche, venture capitalist and author of the State of AI Report. Every year, Nathan and his team compile all the key facts, figures, trends of the AI industry into a 250 slide report that is one of my favorite reads and reference documents. Nathan is back for a third time on this show and as usual, we covered many of the stories of the year as well as some of his predictions. Why AGI could happen in 2027, AI that is now building AI, what really happened in the Hugging Face incident, the data center backlash, and how he runs his own fund on agents. I'm Matt Turk, and this is the MAD Podcast.

Speaker 2 | 00:56 - 01:16
So every year, you do this big report that we're going to extensively talk about, and you end the report with predictions. And, like, historically, your predictions have been somewhat measured, but this year, you went all out. And the the last prediction is AGI 2027. So, why is that? Unpack that for us.

Speaker 1 | 01:16 - 01:36
Yeah. I mean, it's been like ten years roughly speaking of writing this report. And, you know, originally it was like a year is like long enough time that enough stuff happens that you have, you know, enough content to write the report. And honestly, like this year was really, really hectic. Every other day towards the end of the timeline for publishing, which was like October 8, I had to make updates.
